metadata.title: What Drives Risky Prescription Opioid Use? Evidence from Migration

raw_text.abstract: We develop and estimate a dynamic model of risky prescription opioid use that allows us to unpack the role of person- and place-specific drivers of the opioid epidemic and assess the impact of state opioid policies. Event studies indicate that among adults receiving federal disability insurance from 2006 to 2019, moves to states with higher rates of risky use produce an immediate jump in the probability of risky use, followed by an additional gradual increase for the next several years. Model estimates imply large effects of place on both the likelihood of transitioning to addiction and the availability of prescription opioids; they also indicate that these place effects change significantly when state laws restricting pain clinics are enacted. A one standard deviation reduction in all place effects would have reduced risky use by about 40% over our study period. One particular source of place effects, pain clinic laws, reduced risky use by 5%, but could have reduced it by 30% if they had been enacted earlier, with much of this magnification operating through the dynamics of addiction.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: indicator for average daily morphine-equivalent dose (MED) exceeding 120 mg in any calendar quarter of an individual-year, constructed from Medicare Part D prescription claims
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: move to a destination state with higher non-mover risky-use rate than the origin state, defined from annual state-of-residence in SSDI administrative records and state-level risky-use rates among non-movers
empirical_analysis.methodology: Event-study evidence from movers across states combined with a dynamic addiction-and-availability model that decomposes person vs place effects and estimates policy impacts of pain-clinic (pill mill) laws using panel prescription data
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: alternative risky-use proxies (multiple prescribers; overlapping prescriptions); alternative geographies (county/commuting zone); balanced panels and alternative move-identification rules; exclusion of major-destination states and special populations (cancer/hospice); alternative samples (elderly Medicare)
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: United States 2006–2019: 20% sample of Medicare beneficiaries whose eligibility is SSDI, linked to Part D claims and residence ZIP/state; mover sample includes individuals who change state exactly once with up to five years pre- and post-move windows; state opioid policy timing including pain-clinic laws
empirical_analysis.control_variables: demographic strata (age bin × race × gender) for matching; calendar-year effects and relative-year effects around moves; baseline opioid history (opioid-naive vs prior user); Medicaid dual-eligibility and other stable program characteristics
subject: Decompose how person factors and place factors jointly drive risky prescription opioid use and quantify how pain-clinic regulations change addiction dynamics and opioid availability.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Bergesio - Optimal insurance design under limited liability.pdf

metadata.title: Optimal insurance design under limited liability

raw_text.abstract: We study optimal demand for insurance in a classical expected utility setting where the insured party has limited liability and has access to three different types of progressively more restrictive contracts. At one end, with no restrictions on the indemnity schedule, it is optimal to fully insure certain losses while leaving others uninsured. At the other end, if indemnity schedules and retained losses are assumed to be increasing functions of the underlying loss, the optimal insurance policies are shown to be capped deductibles. For the intermediate case when the indemnity schedule is only an increasing function of the loss, we find that optimal contracts exhibit a richer structure beyond the capped policies suggested in earlier literature. Our study extends and provides a unifying perspective on the existing literature on optimal insurance under limited liability.
raw_text.keywords_text: expected utility, insurance, limited liability, optimal demand

theoretical_summary: In an expected-utility model with limited liability, optimal insurance contracts depend on contract-shape restrictions, ranging from selective full insurance to capped deductibles and richer increasing-indemnity structures.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Beyer - Gambling for market recovery  European insurers  corporate bond investments during.pdf

metadata.title: Gambling for market recovery? European insurers' corporate bond investments during market stress

raw_text.abstract: Using daily stock market data for European insurers, I investigate how a stock market contraction, as experienced during the COVID‐19 pandemic, affects insurers' credit risk allocation of their corporate bond portfolio. I find that insurers shift their portfolio holdings pro‐cyclically towards lower credit risk assets in the first month of the market contraction. As the crisis progresses, I find evidence for counter‐cyclical, riskier investment behavior by European insurers, especially in high‐yield instruments, that can neither be explained by credit rating downgrades of held bonds nor by hedging with CDS derivatives. This counter‐cyclical investment behavior cannot be observed for US firms, which provides evidence for a difference in investment behavior between US and European insurers. The observed investment behavior of European insurers could be beneficial for systemic stability by attenuating price declines through insurance liquidity provision, but excessive risk‐taking by insurance companies over longer periods can also reinforce systemic stress.
raw_text.keywords_text: financial crisis, financial stability, insurance

empirical_analysis.methodology: infer intra-quarter portfolio reallocation using rolling regressions of insurer stock returns on bond-index returns by credit rating while controlling for market, volatility, macro variables, and business-line mix; compare to analogous U.S. implementation where holdings are observable

empirical_analysis.control_variables: market index returns, volatility index, exchange rates, inflation, short-rate measures, firm size, liquidity, unit-linked share, and line-of-business premium shares
subject: Measure how European insurers’ corporate-bond risk allocation changes during the COVID-19 market contraction and whether behavior differs from U.S. insurers.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Braun - Extreme‐weather risk and the cross‐section of stock returns.pdf

metadata.title: Extreme-weather risk and the cross-section of stock returns

raw_text.abstract: We document an extreme‐weather risk premium in the cross‐section of stock returns. Between 1995 and 2019, stocks of domestic U.S. firms with the most negative sensitivity to aggregate storm losses earned an annual excess‐return spread of more than 6 percentage points relative to those with the most positive sensitivity, a difference not explained by standard factors. Fama‐MacBeth regressions confirm that more negative storm‐risk betas predict higher subsequent returns. The premium concentrates in geographically exposed and historically affected firms and in institutionally held stocks, consistent with fundamental‐risk and salience channels. Our results establish a link between physical climate risk, the cost of equity, and ultimately firm value.
raw_text.keywords_text: cost of equity, empirical asset pricing, extreme-weather risk

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: firm-level sensitivity to aggregate storm-loss growth (LSLG beta) estimated from 60-month rolling regressions of stock excess returns on LSLG plus standard equity factors
empirical_analysis.methodology: construct aggregate storm-loss growth from SHELDUS; estimate firm storm-risk betas; test pricing via value-weighted beta-sorted portfolios and cross-sectional predictive regressions with extensive factor spanning
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: factor-model spanning with alternative risk factors (liquidity, sentiment, crash-risk, downside market risk, oil, betting-against-beta, reversal, profitability/investment); seasonality controls; subgroup tests by geographic exposure, prior storm mentions, and institutional ownership
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. domestic firms (≥90% U.S. sales) from 01/1995–12/2019; CRSP/Compustat merged data with SHELDUS thunderstorm property+crop losses per capita to form monthly LSLG
empirical_analysis.control_variables: firm size, book-to-market, market beta, idiosyncratic volatility, coskewness, short-term reversal, momentum, and lagged seasonal return controls
subject: Test whether firms more adversely exposed to aggregate storm losses earn higher expected stock returns, indicating an extreme-weather risk premium in equities.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Cassidy - Pollution liability insurance and corporate environmental compliance in China.pdf

metadata.title: Pollution liability insurance and corporate environmental compliance in China

raw_text.abstract: This study examines the effect of a pollution liability insurance mandate on corporate environmental compliance in Shenzhen, China. We employ a triple differences design, comparing electroplating and circuit board (ECB) manufacturing firms, mandated to purchase insurance, to industries and a neighboring city without the mandate. Results show a 0.48 reduction in annual environmental violations per firm (a 72% decrease) across all Shenzhen ECB firms. Within the Shenzhen ECB industry, only about half of firms comply. Notably, both insured and uninsured firms reduced violations, consistent with anticipation that (eventual) premiums would depend on past violations. The insurance could generate two opposing forces: premium‐based incentives to reduce violations versus moral hazard among the insured. We find suggestive evidence that insured firms' environmental compliance gains are partially offset by moral hazard. Our findings demonstrate that premium‐based incentives dominate and effectively counteract market failures due to asymmetric information, increasing environmental compliance on net.
raw_text.keywords_text: adverse selection, environmental compliance, moral hazard, pollution liability insurance

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: policy exposure indicator for Shenzhen electroplating/circuit-board sector after the 2012 mandate introduction (Shenzhen × ECB × Post) with Dongguan and non-mandated industries as controls
empirical_analysis.methodology: triple-differences design across city (Shenzhen vs Dongguan), industry (ECB vs paper/textiles), and time (post vs pre), with fixed effects; within-ECB analysis comparing insured vs uninsured firms to separate premium-incentive and moral-hazard components

empirical_analysis.control_variables: city×year, sector×year, and city×sector fixed effects (and firm fixed effects in robustness); sample restrictions addressing enforcement changes and closures
subject: Estimate whether mandating pollution liability insurance increases corporate environmental compliance by reducing firms’ environmental violations in Shenzhen’s ECB sector.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Chong - Cyber risk assessment for capital management.pdf

metadata.title: Cyber risk assessment for capital management

raw_text.abstract: This paper introduces a two‐pillar cyber risk management framework to address the pervasive challenges in managing cyber risk. The first pillar, cyber risk assessment, combines insurance frequency‐severity models with cybersecurity cascade models to capture the unique nature of cyber risk. The second pillar, cyber capital management, facilitates informed allocation of capital for a balanced cyber risk management strategy, including cybersecurity investments, insurance coverage, and reserves. A case study, based on historical cyber incident data and realistic assumptions, demonstrates the necessity of comprehensive cost–benefit analysis for budget‐constrained companies with competing objectives in cyber risk management. In addition, sensitivity analysis highlights the dependence of the optimal strategy on factors such as the price of cybersecurity controls and their effectiveness. The framework's implementation across a diverse range of companies yields general insights on cyber risk management.
raw_text.keywords_text: cascade model, cyber capital management, cyber risk assessment, cybersecurity investment, insurance coverage and reserve

theoretical_summary: A two-pillar framework integrates a cyber cascade loss model with a capital-allocation problem to jointly optimize cybersecurity investment, insurance coverage, and reserves under budget constraints.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Côté - A fair price to pay  Exploiting causal graphs for fairness in insurance.pdf

metadata.title: A fair price to pay: Exploiting causal graphs for fairness in insurance

raw_text.abstract: In many jurisdictions, insurance companies are prohibited from discriminating based on certain policyholder characteristics. Exclusion of prohibited variables from models prevents direct discrimination, but fails to address proxy discrimination, a phenomenon especially prevalent when powerful predictive algorithms are fed with an abundance of acceptable covariates. The lack of formal definition for key fairness concepts, in particular indirect discrimination, hinders effective fairness assessment. We review causal inference notions and introduce a causal graph tailored for fairness in insurance. Exploiting these, we discuss potential sources of bias, formally define direct and indirect discrimination, and study the theoretical properties of fairness methodologies. A novel categorization of fair methodologies into five families (best-estimate, unaware, aware, hyperaware, and corrective) is constructed based on their expected fairness properties. A comprehensive pedagogical example illustrates the implications of our findings: the interplay between our fair score families, group fairness criteria, and discrimination.
raw_text.keywords_text: bias, causal inference, directed acyclic graph, discrimination, disparate impact, fairness criteria, score

theoretical_summary: A causal-graph framework for insurance pricing formalizes direct and indirect discrimination and classifies fairness methods into five score families with distinct expected fairness properties.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Fang - Shared exposures or management fashions  Antecedents of convergence in the insurance.pdf

metadata.title: Shared exposures or management fashions? Antecedents of convergence in the insurance and banking industries

raw_text.abstract: We study convergence in the attention of decision-makers across the insurance and banking industries. Our analysis is based on textual risk disclosures (10-K reports, 2006–2018), providing a snapshot of corporate priorities and contexts. We theoretically link convergence with decision-making contexts via the Attention-Based View. Leveraging strategic management theory, we identify antecedents of convergence in attention and, therefore, potentially, risk contagion. These include common trends in the macro-environment, substitution threats, and management fashions. We combine this theoretical framework with machine learning tools to create quantitative measures of convergence in attention and its antecedents. We find that the proposed measure of convergence is predictive of inter- and intra-industry stock correlations. Finally, based on regression and sensitivity analyses, we identify the relative importance of different antecedents, showing that shared risk management fashions largely drive inter-industry convergence in attention. This highlights challenges when interpreting regulatory text data in the context of predicting contagion risk.
raw_text.keywords_text: contagion, industry convergence, management attention, risk disclosure, systemic risk, text analysis

empirical_analysis.methodology: construct document embeddings from 10-K Risk Factors text, compute cross-industry and within-industry attention convergence, then evaluate predictive power for future stock correlations and decompose drivers using topic measures from Business sections and nonlinear predictive models with sensitivity analysis
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: alternative predictive models (regularized linear, random forest, gradient boosting) with cross-validation; alternative convergence definitions (within-industry cohesion); sensitivity diagnostics (ALE, feature importance, Shapley)
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. NYSE-listed banks and insurers, 10-K filings 2006–2018 (Risk Factors and Business sections) plus daily stock returns and S&P industry indices for subsequent-year correlations; auxiliary 10-K corpus for pharmaceuticals to proxy management fashions
empirical_analysis.control_variables: year and industry fixed effects in prediction models; document availability indicators; industry subcategory controls (life, P&C, multiline, reinsurance) in extensions
subject: Measure cross-industry convergence in insurers’ and banks’ risk-manager attention using 10-K text and test whether convergence predicts stock co-movement and which contextual forces drive it.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Kramer - Basis risk  social comparison  perceptions of fairness  and demand for insurance  A.pdf

metadata.title: Basis risk, social comparison, perceptions of fairness, and demand for insurance: A field experiment in Ethiopia

raw_text.abstract: Index insurance lowers agricultural risk but covers only covariate risks. Since farmers do not have complete insurance, they may develop mistrust of insurance when experiencing crop losses and not receiving payouts. Although recent innovations in remote sensing enable the provision of more complete insurance including coverage for idiosyncratic risks, such insurance introduces differences in payouts within social networks, which might be considered unfair, introduce jealousy, and depress insurance demand. We conduct a lab‐in‐the‐field experiment with farmers in Ethiopia to examine whether providing complete insurance coverage affects perceived fairness and insurance demand. We also examine effects of informing farmers about neighbors' payout experiences. We find that such social comparison increases perceived fairness of index insurance. Providing complete crop insurance increases perceived fairness of outcomes and willingness to pay for insurance, without introducing jealousy over neighbors receiving different payouts. These results are concentrated among men and those with little insurance knowledge.
raw_text.keywords_text: basis risk, Ethiopia, social comparison, weather index insurance

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: maximum willingness to pay for the offered crop insurance product elicited via an incentivized multiple price list with a randomly drawn premium determining purchase
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator for insurance design that eliminates downside idiosyncratic basis risk (index insurance plus plot-level verification/picture-based fail-safe) versus standard index-only coverage
empirical_analysis.methodology: lab-in-the-field decision tasks with randomized insurance design and randomized presentation of own-versus-neighbor outcomes to test how payout dispersion and comparison affect perceived fairness and demand
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: subgroup analyses by gender and baseline insurance knowledge; alternative specifications controlling for balance covariates and risk/time preferences; checks using fairness-perception outcomes across multiple scenarios
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Ethiopia (Amhara region), June 2021: 480 smallholder farmers in 12 villages; incentivized games on teff insurance with randomized treatments and post-task preference elicitation
empirical_analysis.control_variables: respondent demographics, prior insurance experience, baseline insurance knowledge, risk and time preferences, and village fixed effects where applicable
subject: Estimate how reducing downside basis risk and enabling social comparisons changes perceived fairness and willingness to pay for crop insurance among Ethiopian farmers.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Gupta - Regulating risk culture in the insurance industry using machine learning.pdf

metadata.title: Regulating risk culture in the insurance industry using machine learning

raw_text.abstract: This study examines the relationship between risk culture and regulation in the insurance industry using textual analysis and machine learning. By analyzing 10‐K disclosures, we classify firms into distinct risk culture clusters and find that the risk culture of insurance firms is significantly shaped by their uncertain risk strategies, constraints in defining, implementing, and reporting risks, as well as litigious decisions and risk management practices. A temporal prediction analysis indicates that large insurers maintaining a poor risk culture trend are less likely to reverse it compared to those improving. Moreover, insurance firms show enhanced risk culture post‐Dodd–Frank Act. Our findings underscore the potential benefits of regulations aimed at monitoring and overseeing insurers' risk practices.
raw_text.keywords_text: insurance regulation, risk culture, Dodd–Frank Act, 10-K disclosures

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: post–Dodd–Frank period indicator and related federal oversight environment contrasted with earlier periods using filing-year windows
empirical_analysis.methodology: construct firm-year risk-culture features from annual disclosures, assign firms to culture classes, track transitions over time, and compare culture trends across regulatory eras and insurer size groups

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Hanika - Market discipline in life insurance  Does public risk disclosure encourage less.pdf

metadata.title: Market discipline in life insurance: Does public risk disclosure encourage less risky management actions?

raw_text.abstract: We analyze how public risk disclosure, specifically Solvency II, impacts life insurers' risk‐taking behavior. Using data from 58 German life insurers from 2016 to 2023, we find that publicly reported solvency ratios can affect premium growth and surrender rates. Moreover, insurers appear to improve their solvency ratios following a decline in the previous year. To investigate whether policyholder behavior drives a life insurer's reduced risk‐taking, we then develop a model in which a life insurer seeks to maximize shareholder value. Unlike previous research, we consider annually disclosed solvency ratios, affecting policyholders' dynamic purchase and surrender behavior. In our model, the insurer acts less riskily (e.g., holds more reserves and sells less‐risky insurance portfolios) to maintain higher solvency ratios and mitigate policyholders' adverse reactions. Our findings motivate public risk disclosure to strengthen market discipline, but its level and design must be carefully calibrated to be effective and avoid undue costs.
raw_text.keywords_text: life insurance, market discipline, risk disclosure, Solvency II

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: annual surrender rate (early terminations/surrenders/paid-up conversions as a percent of sum insured) and premium growth from supervisory reports
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: publicly disclosed Solvency II solvency ratio (basic own funds divided by solvency capital requirement) from annual SFCR filings
empirical_analysis.methodology: link annual public solvency disclosures to customer behavior outcomes (premium growth and surrenders) and examine insurer adjustments in subsequent solvency; interpret mechanisms with a multi-period asset–liability model where disclosure affects demand and surrender behavior
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: separate analyses by low vs high solvency-ratio insurers; dynamic specifications that account for persistence in premiums/surrenders; sensitivity to excluding atypical business changes and run-off firms
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Germany, 2016–2023: 58 life insurers (majority of market premium volume) with solvency ratios from SFCRs and firm outcomes from BaFin supervisory data
empirical_analysis.control_variables: firm fixed effects, year effects, log premiums, cost ratios, and insurer type indicators (stock vs mutual)

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Harrison - Welfare consequences of the compound risks of index insurance.pdf

metadata.title: Welfare consequences of the compound risks of index insurance

raw_text.abstract: Index insurance is an attractive variant on the standard insurance contract that allows the determination of a loss event to be defined by one or more thresholds on an index that is positively correlated with actual losses. Index insurance also comes with a compound risk, basis risk. We examine how these compound risks for index insurance affect behavior towards the decision to purchase the product or not. Using incentivized experiments, we control the actuarial specifics of contracts offered, the information provided to decision makers, and our knowledge of the risk preferences of decision makers. We demonstrate that individuals that fail to process compound risks, end up purchasing the contract more than other individuals, as well as more than they should, generating significant welfare losses. We also develop a natural information treatment that mitigates these welfare losses.
raw_text.keywords_text: compound risk, consumer surplus, index insurance, basis risk

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: binary insurance take-up choice across 54 contract decisions per subject (buy vs not buy)
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: information architecture that displays actuarially equivalent reduced-form probabilities for all outcome states (decision aid) versus presenting component probabilities only
empirical_analysis.methodology: incentivized laboratory insurance-choice tasks with controlled loss probability, loss size, premium, and index matching probability; measure individual processing of compound risk via consistency with compound-lottery reduction and evaluate welfare using certainty-equivalent differences
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: subgroup comparisons by compound-risk processing ability; alternative welfare priors under different risk-preference models; sensitivity to contract-parameter subsets and excluding inattentive subjects

empirical_analysis.control_variables: individual risk-preference parameters (utility curvature and probability weighting) and indicators for compound-risk processing consistency

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Jia - Catastrophe risk sharing among individuals  private insurance  and government.pdf

metadata.title: Catastrophe risk sharing among individuals, private insurance, and government

raw_text.abstract: Limited research has been conducted on the optimal public–private risk‐sharing for catastrophe risks. This paper develops a theoretical framework to study the risk‐sharing decisions and interactions of three types of catastrophe‐market participants: a large number of individuals, a large number of private insurers in a competitive market, and a government that can choose between alternatives of re/insurance or ex post relief. Our analysis shows that the optimal government intervention varies depending on the correlation levels among individual losses. For moderately positive levels of loss correlation, it is optimal for the government to offer an ex post relief program to supplement private insurance. However, for higher levels of loss correlation, government reinsurance becomes optimal, although not to the extent of replacing private insurance if the government is less efficient than private firms. In sum, as catastrophe‐loss correlations increase, that is, as the risk becomes more catastrophic, more risk‐sharing tools and funding are needed to maximize social welfare.
raw_text.keywords_text: catastrophe risk management, efficient risk sharing, public–private partnership

theoretical_summary: A social-planner and market-equilibrium framework with individuals, competitive insurers, and a taxing government shows that optimal public intervention shifts from ex post relief to government reinsurance as loss correlation rises, with private insurance generally remaining part of the efficient risk-sharing mix when government operations are less efficient.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Jing - Virtuous innovation or obfuscation  Product innovation in the variable annuities.pdf

metadata.title: Virtuous innovation or obfuscation? Product innovation in the variable annuities market

raw_text.abstract: Variable Annuities, which comprise a substantial proportion of the retirement products sold by insurance companies, have become increasingly complex over the past decades. We investigate the drivers of the product trends. We distinguish “virtuous” innovations that expand upon the existing set of consumption paths in retirement from “obfuscating” innovations that increase complexity without clear benefits to consumers. We document a recurring pattern where, in each benefit category, obfuscating products follow the introduction of virtuous innovations. This pattern generates the overall increase in product complexity. Our results challenge prevailing perspectives on Variable Annuities in the popular press and the literature.
raw_text.keywords_text: variable annuities, financial innovation, product complexity

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Li - Textual analysis of insurance claims with large language models.pdf

metadata.title: Textual analysis of insurance claims with large language models

raw_text.abstract: This study proposes a comprehensive and general framework for examining discrepancies in textual content using large language models (LLMs), broadening application scenarios in the insurtech and risk management fields, and conducting empirical research based on actual needs and real-world data. Our framework integrates OpenAI's interface to embed texts and project them into external categories while utilizing distance metrics to evaluate discrepancies. To identify significant disparities, we design prompts to analyze three types of relationships: identical information, logical relationships, and potential relationships. Our empirical analysis shows that 22.1% of samples exhibit substantial semantic discrepancies, and 38.1% of the samples with significant differences contain at least one of the identified relationships. The average processing time for each sample does not exceed 4 seconds. Backtesting results and comparisons with traditional NLP methods further demonstrate that our proposed method is effective and robust.
raw_text.keywords_text: discrepancy analysis; insurance claim settlement; large language model; risk management

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: semantic discrepancy indicator based on embedding-projection distance metrics (absolute and relative distance on external label projections), with “significant differences” defined by upper quantiles of the distance distribution
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: paired claim-related texts from different sources (e.g., claimant description vs investigator/third-party record) embedded via OpenAI embeddings and projected to the same external label set
empirical_analysis.methodology: embed texts and label categories, compute distance-based discrepancy scores to triage high-discrepancy pairs, then apply structured prompts to classify relationship types between paired texts to guide manual review
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: backtesting with alternative pretrained embedding models and comparisons against traditional similarity baselines; stability checks across discrepancy regions defined by distance quantiles
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Life insurance claim settlement text pairs from China Life Reinsurance Company Ltd., analyzed as a cross-sectional sample of paired documents (study period as provided in the paper’s case study)
empirical_analysis.control_variables: label-set fixed structure; preprocessing controls for text cleaning and segmentation; sensitivity to choice of top-k label projection depth
subject: Detect and interpret meaningful inconsistencies between paired insurance claim texts using LLM-based embeddings, external-label projections, and relationship classification.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Liao - Community responses to flooding in risk mitigation actions  Evidence from the.pdf

metadata.title: Community responses to flooding in risk mitigation actions: Evidence from the community rating system

raw_text.abstract: This paper studies the impact of disaster experiences on communities' engagement in risk mitigation actions, focusing on flooding in the United States. We measure risk mitigation actions using communities' scores in the Community Rating System (CRS), an incentive program that scores flood preparedness and mitigation activities and rewards communities with flood insurance premium discounts. Leveraging a panel of communities from 1998 to 2019, we find a significant increase in risk mitigation activities following flood events, in both participation rates and intensity of actions. The effects continue to increase up to 10 years. Communities with greater capacity, particularly those in urban areas, exhibit a much stronger response.
raw_text.keywords_text: climate adaptation; community action; flood insurance; risk mitigation

raw_text.abstract: Merging building footprints and inundation data for Hurricane Sandy, we document substantial flood risk outside FEMA’s 100-year flood zone and show the storm led to large increases in flood insurance take-up. The increase fades after three years inside the flood zone but is persistent in the periphery, consistent with belief updating among first-time flooded residents outside the mandate area.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Veith - On the market valuation of insurance accounting  An assessment of historical cost.pdf

metadata.title: On the market valuation of insurance accounting: An assessment of historical cost and fair value measurements

raw_text.abstract: We analyze the relationship between stock prices and insurance accounting and compare a historical cost with a full fair value measurement approach. During our sample period, European insurers had to determine the fair value of all assets and liabilities according to the Solvency II (SII) regulation, in addition to the historical‐cost‐based setup of the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). This alternative source of information allowed investors to update their expectations about future dividends, risks, and firm values. Comparing both frameworks, we report three findings. First, we show that the association between stock prices and SII full fair value accounting items is greater than that of IFRS historical cost measurements. Second, we find that this effect stems from unexpected news disclosed by regulatory reporting. Third, our results suggest that insurance accounting is relevant for firms exposed to lower insolvency risk and offers no additional information when the risk level is high.
raw_text.keywords_text: fair value accounting, historical cost accounting, International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), Solvency II (SII)

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: stock price (euros per share) measured 5 days after the IFRS report date and 5 days after the SFCR (Solvency II) publication date for the same fiscal year
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: unexpected Solvency II versus IFRS balance-sheet adjustments computed as residuals from first-stage regressions predicting SII–IFRS differences in net assets (and major items) using IFRS net assets/items, IFRS net income, and the solvency ratio
empirical_analysis.methodology: incremental association price-level valuation framework comparing the association of equity prices with IFRS historical-cost items versus Solvency II full fair-value items and isolating the incremental effect via unexpected (surprise) regulatory disclosures
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: alternative post-disclosure pricing windows (1-day and 10-day), inclusion of intangibles in SII net assets, restricted samples excluding major cross-holdings and non-EU domiciles, and subsample analysis by solvency-risk (median solvency ratio split)
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: 53 listed European insurers with annual IFRS group reports and Solvency II SFCR group reports, fiscal years 2016–2020 (254 firm-year observations) with manual SFCR collection and market data from Refinitiv Datastream
empirical_analysis.control_variables: per-share scaling; country and year fixed effects; firm-level clustered standard errors; winsorization of prices; outlier removal using studentized residual thresholds; conditioning on solvency ratio for risk stratification
subject: Assess whether Solvency II full fair-value regulatory accounting provides incremental information for insurer stock valuation beyond IFRS historical-cost accounting, and whether this depends on solvency risk.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Wan - Demand for life annuities  critical illness insurance  and long‐term care insurance.pdf

metadata.title: Demand for life annuities, critical illness insurance, and long-term care insurance

raw_text.abstract: We develop a rich life-cycle model to assess the demand for life annuities, critical illness insurance, and long-term care (LTC) insurance by retirees in a portfolio-allocation setting. We calibrate our model to urban China, where retirees face limited public insurance and undeveloped private markets. We show that retirees with a low public pension should allocate at least 30% of their financial wealth at retirement to a life annuity. Those with an average pension should allocate at least 30% to critical illness insurance. The allocation to LTC insurance ranges from 5% to 33% across all economic profiles considered. Access to critical illness and LTC insurance does not necessarily increase annuity demand. However, access to annuities decreases LTC insurance demand. Our results suggest that countries with limited public insurance should first ensure the adequacy of retirement income and then focus on covering catastrophic medical expenses while providing basic LTC services for all.
raw_text.keywords_text: annuity, critical illness insurance, long term care insurance, life cycle saving, retirement

theoretical_summary: A calibrated retirement life-cycle model for urban China shows optimal portfolio allocations across annuities, critical illness insurance, and LTC insurance depend on pension adequacy and wealth, with product interactions implying health-contingent insurance can crowd out annuities and annuities can reduce LTC insurance demand.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Yu - Ship insurance in the era of AI  An intelligent risk profiling system under the POM.pdf

metadata.title: Ship insurance in the era of AI: An intelligent risk profiling system under the POM principles

raw_text.abstract: As the origin of modern commercial insurance, ship insurance underpins global maritime supply chain stability. Yet shipping modernization and AI advances expose three flaws in traditional risk profiling: misalignment with frequency-severity pricing, inadequate for accommodating to complex risk factor system, and lack of data stream adjustment mechanisms. To address these, we propose POM principles (Personalized risk portrait, Omnispective risk factors, and Maneuverable calibration) and an AI framework with three cores: (1) extensible “retrospective + prospective” risk factors; (2) independent AI modules for premium rate/insurance amount prediction; (3) data steam calibration on historical data. Validated via 15,007 records (15% of China's 2016–2021 registered ships) using random forest regression, it outperforms traditional generalized linear models and mainstream machine learning models in accuracy and risk differentiation. This pioneers intelligent ship insurance profiling, fills gaps in individualized pricing, and offers insights for sectors like aviation insurance, sharing its “premium rate × insurance amount” logic.
raw_text.keywords_text: intelligent risk profiling, machine learning, premium rate, risk factors, ship insurance

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: policy premium rate (‱) observed at underwriting date and an actuarially calibrated premium rate adjusted via earned-premium loss-ratio bounds using window-level scaling rules; parallel target includes insurance amount from policy records
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: ship-level retrospective and prospective drivers measured at policy inception, including ship registry tonnage, ship age, ship type, classification society, navigation area, builder country, prior-year loss ratio, prior-year accidents and accident type, enterprise ownership, and market indices (China SSPI and CSPI)
empirical_analysis.methodology: train separate random-forest regression models to predict (i) calibrated premium rates and (ii) insurance amounts under a POM-guided framework, combining an actuarial data-stream calibration step (loss-ratio banding) with individualized factor-based prediction and benchmarking against GLMs and alternative ML models
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: stability tests using annual cumulative samples and repeated train/test splits; alternative model benchmarks (decision tree, gradient boosting, LightGBM, XGBoost, Gaussian/Gamma GLMs); robustness of risk-differentiation using ordered Lorenz curves, Gini indices, and lift metrics; feature-importance stability over time
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: China ship insurance policies 2016–2021 (15,007 ship records from three insurers; ~15% of registered ships), with claims observed through 2022 for loss-ratio calibration and ship-market indices (SSPI, CSPI) for prospective factors
empirical_analysis.control_variables: ship type and navigation-area categories, ownership types, prior experience measures, and market-index levels at inception; consistent inception-time measurement to avoid forward-looking covariates
subject: Develop and validate an AI-based ship-insurance risk profiling system that predicts premium rates and insurance amounts using ship-level characteristics and shipping-market signals while calibrating historical premium data to actuarial loss-ratio targets.
